# Part 2 — Citation graph: structural descriptions

## Setup

```{r}
#| label: install
#| eval: false
install.packages(c("igraph", "tidyverse", "ggraph", "tidygraph", "jsonlite"))
```

```{r}
#| label: libraries
library(igraph)
library(tidyverse)
library(ggraph)
library(tidygraph)
library(jsonlite)
library(here)
```

```{r}
#| label: load-graph
edges <- read_csv(here("data", "citation_edgelist.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE)
g <- graph_from_data_frame(edges, directed = TRUE)

bib <- fromJSON(here("data", "bibliography.json"), simplifyDataFrame = FALSE)

# Active entries only (tombstoned entries are excluded from the export,
# but guard here in case of an older bibliography file). Note: entries
# tombstoned via `delete` (not `merge`) that appear as a citer elsewhere
# are retained in the edge list so their outbound edges aren't lost — see
# exporter.py and docs/methods/corrections-system.md. Ghost nodes have no
# reliable bibliographic metadata; they are kept in the graph (their edges
# are real) but excluded from any display table or join that assumes real
# title/author/topic data.
bib <- bib[!sapply(bib, function(e) isTRUE(e[["_deleted"]]))]

node_attrs <- tibble(
  name            = names(bib),
  title           = map_chr(bib, ~ .x$title %||% ""),
  year            = map_chr(bib, ~ .x$date %||% .x$year %||% ""),
  generation      = map_chr(bib, ~ .x$generation %||% ""),
  entry_type      = map_chr(bib, ~ .x$entry_type %||% ""),
  resolution      = map_chr(bib, ~ .x[["_resolution_method"]] %||% "grobid"),
  completeness    = map_chr(bib, ~ .x$completeness$label %||% ""),
)

# Ghost = a node present in the edge list (it cites or is cited by
# something) but absent from the active bibliography — i.e. no real
# metadata to join. Derived from edge-list membership rather than a
# GraphML attribute, since we're not loading GraphML at all (libxml2
# isn't installable here without sudo — see gn_analysis/README.md for
# the same constraint on the GN side).
is_ghost <- tibble(
  name     = V(g)$name,
  is_ghost = if_else(V(g)$name %in% node_attrs$name, "false", "true")
)

cat("Nodes:", vcount(g), "\n")
cat("Edges:", ecount(g), "\n")
cat("Directed:", is_directed(g), "\n")
cat("Density:", edge_density(g), "\n")
cat("Ghost nodes (tombstoned entries retained for edge preservation):",
    sum(is_ghost$is_ghost == "true"), "\n")
```

## Degree and centrality

In-degree (times cited within the corpus) and out-degree (number of works
cited) capture different roles. High in-degree identifies widely-cited works
— the intellectual anchors of the field. High out-degree identifies works
that are heavily engaged with the literature, drawing on many sources.

Betweenness centrality identifies works that sit on many shortest paths
between other works — brokers between sub-literatures. Betweenness is
expensive to compute on large graphs; normalized values are reported.

PageRank assigns authority based on incoming links weighted by the
authority of the linking node — conceptually similar to being cited by
works that are themselves widely cited. Hub and authority scores (HITS)
are complementary: hubs point to many authorities; authorities are pointed
to by many hubs.

Peripheral works — low degree, low centrality by every measure below — are
not treated as noise in this project. A work cited only once may be exactly
the interesting case (a niche, contested, or newly emerging reference) for
a study of citational politics. No node is excluded from any measure in
this section on the basis of low degree.

```{r}
#| label: degree
V(g)$degree_in  <- degree(g, mode = "in")
V(g)$degree_out <- degree(g, mode = "out")
V(g)$degree_all <- degree(g, mode = "all")
```

```{r}
#| label: centrality
V(g)$betweenness  <- betweenness(g, directed = TRUE, normalized = TRUE)
V(g)$closeness_in <- closeness(g, mode = "in", normalized = TRUE)
V(g)$pagerank     <- page_rank(g, directed = TRUE)$vector
V(g)$hub          <- hub_score(g)$vector
V(g)$authority    <- authority_score(g)$vector

centrality_df <- tibble(
  name        = V(g)$name,
  betweenness = V(g)$betweenness,
  closeness   = V(g)$closeness_in,
  pagerank    = V(g)$pagerank,
  hub         = V(g)$hub,
  authority   = V(g)$authority,
  in_degree   = V(g)$degree_in,
  out_degree  = V(g)$degree_out,
  degree      = V(g)$degree_all,
) |> left_join(node_attrs, by = "name") |> left_join(is_ghost, by = "name")
```

### Most cited (by in-degree)

```{r}
centrality_df |>
  filter(is_ghost == "false") |>
  arrange(desc(in_degree)) |>
  head(20) |>
  select(name, title, year, generation, in_degree) |>
  knitr::kable()
```

### Most citing (by out-degree)

```{r}
centrality_df |>
  filter(is_ghost == "false") |>
  arrange(desc(out_degree)) |>
  head(20) |>
  select(name, title, year, generation, out_degree) |>
  knitr::kable()
```

### Degree distribution

A power-law or scale-free degree distribution is characteristic of citation
networks: most works are cited rarely, a small number are cited frequently.
The log-log plot tests this.

```{r}
#| label: degree-dist
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 5
ggplot(centrality_df, aes(x = in_degree)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 50, fill = "steelblue") +
  scale_x_log10() +
  scale_y_log10() +
  labs(
    title = "In-degree distribution (log-log)",
    x = "In-degree (times cited)",
    y = "Count"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

### Top by betweenness centrality

Works with high betweenness mediate between otherwise disconnected parts
of the citation network — likely works that bridge sub-fields or periods.

```{r}
centrality_df |>
  filter(is_ghost == "false") |>
  arrange(desc(betweenness)) |>
  head(20) |>
  select(name, title, year, betweenness) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 4)
```

## Connected components

A weakly connected component (WCC) treats edges as undirected. A strongly
connected component (SCC) requires paths in both directions — rare in
citation networks, since citations are historically directed (a 2010 paper
cannot cite a 2020 paper). The WCC structure shows how fragmented the
network is; a dominant giant component indicates a well-connected literature.

```{r}
#| label: components
wcc <- components(g, mode = "weak")
scc <- components(g, mode = "strong")

cat("Weakly connected components:", wcc$no, "\n")
cat("Largest WCC:", max(wcc$csize), "nodes (",
    round(100 * max(wcc$csize) / vcount(g), 1), "% of graph)\n")
cat("Strongly connected components:", scc$no, "\n")
cat("Largest SCC:", max(scc$csize), "nodes\n")

V(g)$component_weak   <- wcc$membership
V(g)$component_strong <- scc$membership
```

### WCC size distribution

```{r}
tibble(size = wcc$csize) |>
  count(size) |>
  arrange(desc(size)) |>
  head(20) |>
  knitr::kable()
```

## K-core decomposition

The k-core of a graph is the maximal subgraph in which every node has at
least k connections to other nodes within that subgraph. It is computed by
iteratively removing nodes with degree below k until no further removal
is possible. Nodes are assigned a coreness value equal to the highest k
for which they remain in the k-core.

K-core decomposition is reported here purely as a **descriptive** measure —
identifying which works are structurally embedded in dense mutual-citation
relationships versus which sit at the periphery. It is not used below as a
preprocessing filter for any other method; every peripheral node (coreness
= 1, or excluded entirely from any k ≥ 2 core) remains a full participant in
every other analysis in this document, including Girvan-Newman.

Reference: Alvarez-Hamelin et al. (2005). Large scale networks
fingerprinting and visualization using the k-core decomposition.
*Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems*, 18.

```{r}
#| label: kcore
g_undirected <- as.undirected(g, mode = "collapse")
V(g)$coreness <- coreness(g_undirected)

cat("Coreness distribution:\n")
table(V(g)$coreness) |> print()

centrality_df <- centrality_df |>
  left_join(tibble(name = V(g)$name, coreness = V(g)$coreness), by = "name")

centrality_df |>
  group_by(coreness) |>
  summarise(n = n(), mean_in_degree = mean(in_degree)) |>
  arrange(desc(coreness)) |>
  head(15) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 2)
```

```{r}
#| label: kcore-top
centrality_df |>
  filter(is_ghost == "false") |>
  arrange(desc(coreness), desc(in_degree)) |>
  head(20) |>
  select(name, title, year, coreness, in_degree) |>
  knitr::kable()
```

## Community detection

Community detection here produces several independent descriptions of how
the graph divides, not a single answer to be triangulated (see "Core
methodological stance" above). Louvain and Leiden ask "which groups of
nodes are more densely interconnected than a random graph with the same
degree sequence would predict." Girvan-Newman asks "which edges, if
removed, disconnect otherwise-separate parts of the network." These are
genuinely different questions; neither validates the other.

References:

- Blondel et al. (2008). Fast unfolding of communities in large networks.
  *Journal of Statistical Mechanics*, P10008.
- Traag et al. (2019). From Louvain to Leiden. *Scientific Reports*, 9, 5233.
- Girvan & Newman (2002). Community structure in social and biological
  networks. *PNAS*, 99(12), 7821–7826.
- Newman (2006). Modularity and community structure in networks.
  *PNAS*, 103(23), 8577–8582.

```{r}
#| label: louvain
louvain <- cluster_louvain(g_undirected)
cat("Louvain communities:", length(louvain), "\n")
cat("Modularity:", round(modularity(louvain), 4), "\n")
V(g)$community_louvain <- membership(louvain)

tibble(community = seq_along(sizes(louvain)), size = sizes(louvain)) |>
  arrange(desc(size)) |>
  head(20) |>
  knitr::kable()
```

```{r}
#| label: louvain-viz
#| fig-width: 12
#| fig-height: 12
#| cache: true
tg <- as_tbl_graph(g) |>
  activate(nodes) |>
  mutate(community = as.factor(V(g)$community_louvain))

ggraph(tg, layout = "drl") +
  geom_edge_link(alpha = 0.05, colour = "grey60") +
  geom_node_point(aes(colour = community), size = 0.3, alpha = 0.7) +
  scale_colour_viridis_d(guide = "none") +
  theme_graph() +
  labs(title = "Citation graph — Louvain communities")

ggsave("bibvik_louvain.png", width = 16, height = 16, dpi = 300)
ggsave("bibvik_louvain.pdf", width = 16, height = 16, device = cairo_pdf)
```

```{r}
#| label: leiden
leiden <- cluster_leiden(g_undirected, objective_function = "modularity")
cat("Leiden communities:", length(leiden), "\n")
leiden_membership <- as.integer(membership(leiden))
cat("Modularity:", round(modularity(g_undirected, leiden_membership), 4), "\n")
V(g)$community_leiden <- leiden_membership

tibble(community = seq_along(sizes(leiden)), size = sizes(leiden)) |>
  arrange(desc(size)) |>
  head(20) |>
  knitr::kable()
```

```{r}
#| label: leiden-viz
#| fig-width: 12
#| fig-height: 12
#| cache: true
tg <- as_tbl_graph(g) |>
  activate(nodes) |>
  mutate(community = as.factor(V(g)$community_leiden))

ggraph(tg, layout = "drl") +
  geom_edge_link(alpha = 0.05, colour = "grey60") +
  geom_node_point(aes(colour = community), size = 0.3, alpha = 0.7) +
  scale_colour_viridis_d(guide = "none") +
  theme_graph() +
  labs(title = "Citation graph — Leiden communities")

ggsave("bibvik_leiden.png", width = 16, height = 16, dpi = 300)
ggsave("bibvik_leiden.pdf", width = 16, height = 16, device = cairo_pdf)
```

## K-means clustering

K-means clusters nodes based on their centrality feature profiles rather
than graph structure. It groups works that occupy similar structural
positions — for example, highly-cited authorities vs. high-betweenness
brokers vs. peripheral works — rather than groups that densely cite each
other. This is a further independent description, not a validation of the
community-detection methods above.

```{r}
#| label: km
features <- centrality_df |>
  select(betweenness, closeness, pagerank, hub, authority, in_degree) |>
  mutate(across(everything(), ~ replace_na(., 0))) |>
  mutate(across(everything(), ~ scale(.)[,1]))

set.seed(42)
k <- 6
km <- kmeans(features, centers = k, nstart = 25)
centrality_df$cluster_kmeans <- km$cluster
V(g)$cluster_kmeans <- km$cluster

cat("Cluster sizes:\n")
table(km$cluster) |> print()
```

```{r}
#| label: km-viz
#| fig-width: 12
#| fig-height: 12
#| cache: true
tg <- as_tbl_graph(g) |>
  activate(nodes) |>
  mutate(cluster = as.factor(V(g)$cluster_kmeans))

ggraph(tg, layout = "drl") +
  geom_edge_link(alpha = 0.05, colour = "grey60") +
  geom_node_point(aes(colour = cluster), size = 0.3, alpha = 0.7) +
  scale_colour_viridis_d(guide = "none") +
  theme_graph() +
  labs(title = "Citation graph — K-means clusters (by centrality profile)")

ggsave("bibvik_kmeans.png", width = 16, height = 16, dpi = 300)
ggsave("bibvik_kmeans.pdf", width = 16, height = 16, device = cairo_pdf)
```

### Cluster profiles

```{r}
#| label: km-profiles
centrality_df |>
  group_by(cluster_kmeans) |>
  summarise(
    n                = n(),
    mean_pagerank    = mean(pagerank, na.rm = TRUE),
    mean_betweenness = mean(betweenness, na.rm = TRUE),
    mean_authority   = mean(authority, na.rm = TRUE),
    mean_in_degree   = mean(in_degree, na.rm = TRUE),
  ) |>
  arrange(desc(mean_in_degree)) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 5)
```

## Structural node table export

```{r}
#| label: export-structural
node_table <- centrality_df |>
  left_join(
    tibble(
      name              = V(g)$name,
      coreness          = V(g)$coreness,
      component_weak    = V(g)$component_weak,
      component_strong  = V(g)$component_strong,
      community_louvain = V(g)$community_louvain,
      community_leiden  = V(g)$community_leiden,
      cluster_kmeans    = V(g)$cluster_kmeans,
    ),
    by = "name"
  )

# Girvan-Newman communities are computed standalone (see gn_analysis/)
# and joined in here only if available. communities.csv (written by
# run_gn_analysis.R) holds the best-modularity cut, which on this
# corpus is 97.5% singletons and not usable — see the write-up below.
# The partition actually joined here is the earliest fragmentation-onset
# cut from gn_analysis/results/multi_cut/, produced by
# generate_multi_cut_communities.R. That directory holds one file per
# detected onset round; the earliest (smallest round number) is the one
# established below as usable, so it's selected by sorting rather than
# a hardcoded round number, in case a future re-run shifts which rounds
# qualify.
gn_multi_cut_dir <- here("analysis", "gn_analysis", "results", "multi_cut")
gn_cut_files <- if (dir.exists(gn_multi_cut_dir)) {
  list.files(gn_multi_cut_dir, pattern = "^communities_round_[0-9]+\\.csv$", full.names = TRUE)
} else {
  character(0)
}

if (length(gn_cut_files) > 0) {
  gn_rounds <- as.integer(gsub(".*communities_round_([0-9]+)\\.csv$", "\\1", gn_cut_files))
  gn_result_path <- gn_cut_files[which.min(gn_rounds)]
  gn_communities <- read_csv(gn_result_path) |>
    rename(community_gn = community_id)
  node_table <- node_table |> left_join(gn_communities, by = c("name" = "node_id"))
  cat("Joined Girvan-Newman communities from", gn_result_path,
      "(fragmentation-onset round", min(gn_rounds), ") \n")
} else {
  cat("No Girvan-Newman multi-cut results found at", gn_multi_cut_dir,
      "— run gn_analysis/generate_multi_cut_communities.R first. Skipping join.\n")
}

write_csv(node_table, "bibvik_node_table.csv")
cat("Written bibvik_node_table.csv\n")
cat("Rows:", nrow(node_table), "\n")

# Plain boolean, computed once here rather than repeated as a quoted
# expression in each downstream chunk's eval: guard — avoids YAML
# quoting issues with !expr and string literals.
gn_has_communities <- "community_gn" %in% colnames(node_table) && any(!is.na(node_table$community_gn))
```

## Girvan-Newman communities

Computed standalone (see `gn_analysis/README.md`) and joined in above only
if that run's output was available at render time. Summary, size table,
and plot below are shown only if a partition was found in
`gn_analysis/results/multi_cut/`.

**Choosing a stopping point.** Girvan-Newman is a divisive algorithm: it
removes one edge at a time, so the graph passes through every possible
partition from fully connected to fully atomized, and a single partition
must be chosen from that sequence to report as "the communities." The
conventional stopping rule — the round of highest modularity across the
whole run — fails on this corpus: modularity keeps rising as the graph
disintegrates into isolated works, peaking only once 97.5% of nodes are
singleton "communities" of size one. This is a known limitation of
modularity as a stopping criterion on sparse, hub-dominated citation
networks rather than a fault in the computation, but it means the
best-modularity partition cannot be used as reported.

Two alternative stopping criteria were evaluated directly against this
corpus's edge-removal sequence. The first, locating the sharpest single-round
drop in modularity, proved unreliable here: the modularity trace is noisy
throughout the heavily-fragmented tail of the run, so the single steepest
drop falls in that same noisy region rather than at a meaningful
transition. The second — treating the point where the count of connected
components begins rising by roughly one per round, and continues doing so
for a sustained run of 100 or more consecutive rounds — identifies the
onset of active fragmentation directly from the graph's own breakup
behaviour, independent of modularity. This is the criterion used here.
(Percolation-theory measures that track component *size* rather than
component *count* — e.g. a susceptibility statistic, or the rate of
decline of the giant component — were considered as complementary checks
on this choice but have not yet been computed for this corpus.)

Applying the fragmentation-onset criterion to this run's edge-removal
sequence identifies eleven points at which the corpus's fragmentation
rate undergoes a sustained increase, not one: rounds 9,062, 10,837,
11,560, 11,859, 21,451, 21,805, 22,162, 22,524, 22,892, 23,264, and
23,644. As with the previous corpus, this is itself informative about
the corpus's structure — literature does not fragment into communities
in one clean step, but in a series of accelerating breakups. However,
these eleven points are not interchangeable candidates for "the"
community partition:

| Round  | Communities | Singletons | % singleton | Largest community |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 9,062  | 297    | 90    | 30% | 964 |
| 10,837 | 1,449  | 1,165 | 80% | 168 |
| 11,560 | 1,986  | 1,666 | 84% | 96  |
| 11,859 | 2,243  | 1,918 | 86% | 88  |
| 21,451 | 11,570 | 11,224| 97% | 17  |
| 21,805 | 11,902 | 11,556| 97% | 15  |
| 22,162 | 12,237 | 11,891| 97% | 13  |
| 22,524 | 12,575 | 12,229| 97% | 11  |
| 22,892 | 12,919 | 12,573| 97% | 9   |
| 23,264 | 13,267 | 12,921| 97% | 7   |
| 23,644 | 13,620 | 13,274| 97% | 5   |

Unlike the previous corpus, the earliest transition (round 9,062) is
not fully singleton-free: 90 of its 297 communities are singletons.
Checked directly, all 90 have degree exactly 1 in the original,
unfiltered graph — each was connected to only a single other node
before Girvan-Newman removed any edges at all. Their appearance as
singletons this early is therefore a structural property of the
corpus (a set of peripheral, minimally-connected nodes) rather than an
artifact of stopping at this particular round; a later cut would not
have kept them attached to anything more substantial. Every subsequent
transition after round 9,062 is already majority-singleton, worsening
monotonically toward the same near-total-fragmentation state that
ruled out the modularity-peak stopping rule in the first place. The
corpus's later fragmentation points therefore document how community
structure dissolves rather than offering alternative, equally-valid
readings of it. Round 9,062 is used below as the working partition
(`community_gn`); the partitions at the other ten points are retained
in `gn_analysis/results/multi_cut/` as a record of that dissolution,
not as alternative community assignments.

This procedure identifies the coarsest point at which the corpus still
exhibits legible community structure — it does not, on its own,
establish that this is where the *most meaningful* structure lies. An
earlier exploratory pass, on an earlier version of this corpus,
checked two individual communities from a nearby cut against paper
titles and the study's own annotation coding and found the groupings
interpretable (a theory/ritual cluster separating cleanly from a
place-names/hoards cluster within one community, for instance); that
spot-check has not been repeated on this corpus's community
assignments, nor extended systematically across the full partition, so
it supports plausibility rather than confirming that round 9,062 is
uniquely correct. Readers who want a finer-grained or
differently-motivated partition should treat the dendrogram below, not
this flat cut, as the primary source: it preserves the full nested
structure and does not require committing to one round.

**Reading the dendrogram.** `gn_analysis/build_dendrogram.R`
reconstructs the complete nested merge structure from the edge-removal
sequence, rather than the single flat partition above. Its construction
logic was verified against hand-traced synthetic cases and reproduces
the expected leaf and merge counts on this corpus. Height on the plotted
tree reflects merge order rather than raw round number: because splits
are unevenly spaced across the run's ~24,600 rounds, a linear round-based
axis compressed the whole tree into an unreadable band. The real round
underlying each merge is preserved separately (`round_at_height` in the
saved `.rds` object) for anyone who needs actual round distances rather
than sequence order. The six fragmentation points identified above are
not yet marked on the plotted tree.

```{r}
#| label: gn-summary
#| eval: !expr gn_has_communities
gn_sizes <- node_table |>
  filter(!is.na(community_gn)) |>
  count(community_gn, name = "size")

cat("Girvan-Newman communities:", nrow(gn_sizes), "\n")
cat("Modularity:", round(modularity(g_undirected, as.integer(factor(node_table$community_gn))), 4), "\n")

gn_sizes |>
  arrange(desc(size)) |>
  head(20) |>
  knitr::kable()
```

```{r}
#| label: gn-viz
#| fig-width: 12
#| fig-height: 12
#| cache: true
#| eval: !expr gn_has_communities
# 297 communities colored individually via a continuous viridis scale
# is not legible: adjacent community IDs land on near-identical shades,
# so the plot reads as a handful of broad color bands rather than 297
# distinct groups (confirmed visually on a render of the previous
# corpus, at a similar community count). Highlighting only the
# largest communities in distinct colors, with everything else grey,
# shows the actual pattern in this partition instead: a handful of
# large communities against a long tail of small ones.
top_gn_communities <- node_table |>
  filter(!is.na(community_gn)) |>
  count(community_gn, sort = TRUE) |>
  slice_head(n = 12) |>
  pull(community_gn)

tg <- as_tbl_graph(g) |>
  activate(nodes) |>
  left_join(node_table |> select(name, community_gn), by = "name") |>
  mutate(
    community_gn_highlight = if_else(community_gn %in% top_gn_communities,
                                      as.character(community_gn), "other"),
    community_gn_highlight = fct_relevel(community_gn_highlight, "other")
  )

ggraph(tg, layout = "drl") +
  geom_edge_link(alpha = 0.05, colour = "grey60") +
  geom_node_point(aes(colour = community_gn_highlight),
                   size = 0.3, alpha = 0.7) +
  scale_colour_manual(
    values = c("other" = "grey85", setNames(grDevices::hcl(h = seq(15, 375, length.out = 13)[-13],
                                                            c = 100, l = 65), top_gn_communities)),
    guide = "none"
  ) +
  theme_graph() +
  labs(title = "Citation graph — Girvan-Newman communities (fragmentation-onset cut, round 9062)",
       subtitle = "12 largest communities highlighted; remaining 285 shown in grey")

ggsave("bibvik_gn.png", width = 16, height = 16, dpi = 300)
ggsave("bibvik_gn.pdf", width = 16, height = 16, device = cairo_pdf)
```

### Girvan-Newman dendrogram

Built separately by `gn_analysis/build_dendrogram.R` from
`removal_log.csv`. Not part of this render; run manually and embedded
here if present. Shows the earliest split events (coarsest structure);
see the script for the full `split_events.csv` and the `.rds` tree
object if you want to zoom into a subtree.

```{r}
#| label: gn-dendrogram-embed
#| eval: !expr file.exists(here("analysis", "gn_analysis", "results", "dendrogram", "gn_dendrogram.png"))
#| out-width: "100%"
knitr::include_graphics(here("analysis", "gn_analysis", "results", "dendrogram", "gn_dendrogram.png"))
```

### Internal structure of individual communities

The round-9,062 partition and the whole-graph dendrogram above both
describe the corpus at a single level: 297 communities, and one tree
covering the earliest few hundred splits across all of them together.
A separate question is whether any individual community has further
structure worth surfacing on its own, the same kind of check performed
earlier (see "Choosing a stopping point") for two clusters against
paper titles and annotation coding.

`gn_analysis/build_subcluster_trees.R` addresses this directly: seeded
from the real round-9,062 community membership (not a re-derived or
arbitrary starting point), it replays `removal_log.csv` separately for
each of the round's largest communities and records what happens to
each one afterward. An initial version capped this replay at a fixed
number of split events; that cap was itself an arbitrary choice with
no basis in the data, so the script now replays each community to
natural completion (full fragmentation or the end of the log) by
default.

Doing so shows that, past each community's first split, every one of
the twelve largest communities collapses the same way the whole graph
does: a single dominant piece sheds one node at a time for hundreds of
further rounds, with no further balanced division anywhere in the
sequence. Plotted as a dendrogram, this produces the same long
single-branch shape for every community regardless of its size or its
first split, differing only in length, so the per-community dendrogram
plots turned out uninformative and are not included here (the script
still writes them; see `gn_analysis/results/subclusters/` if useful).

The one real signal in this data is the size of the two pieces at each
community's first split, which varies meaningfully across the twelve:
most split off a single node or a small handful, but two communities
(56, with a 111/47 split, and 130, with a 92/53 split) divide into two
pieces of comparable size, the same kind of balanced division that made
the two clusters checked earlier interpretable. One community (19) is a
genuine anomaly rather than a matter of degree: its first split produces
a 10/257 division, the *smaller* piece splitting off first while the
bulk of the community stays together, unlike every other community
here (and every community checked in the previous version of this
corpus), where the smaller piece is the one shed and the bulk always
stays intact on the first split. This has not yet been investigated
further; it may indicate a distinct substructure worth checking against
titles or annotation coding, or it may be an artifact of how this
particular community's internal edges were structured before edge
removal began.

```{r}
#| label: gn-first-splits
#| fig-width: 11
#| fig-height: 6.5
#| eval: !expr file.exists(here("analysis", "gn_analysis", "results", "subclusters", "subcluster_summary.csv"))
subcluster_summary <- read_csv(
  here("analysis", "gn_analysis", "results", "subclusters", "subcluster_summary.csv"),
  show_col_types = FALSE
)

first_splits <- subcluster_summary |>
  filter(!is.na(first_split_sizes)) |>
  separate(first_split_sizes, into = c("piece_a", "piece_b"), sep = "/", convert = TRUE) |>
  mutate(
    larger_piece  = pmax(piece_a, piece_b),
    smaller_piece = pmin(piece_a, piece_b)
  ) |>
  arrange(desc(smaller_piece)) |>
  mutate(community_label = fct_reorder(paste("Community", community_id), smaller_piece))

first_splits_long <- first_splits |>
  select(community_label, larger_piece, smaller_piece) |>
  pivot_longer(c(larger_piece, smaller_piece), names_to = "piece", values_to = "size") |>
  mutate(piece = factor(piece, levels = c("larger_piece", "smaller_piece"),
                         labels = c("Larger piece", "Smaller piece")))

ggplot(first_splits_long, aes(x = size, y = community_label, fill = piece)) +
  geom_col(position = position_dodge(width = 0.7), width = 0.6) +
  geom_text(aes(label = size), position = position_dodge(width = 0.7),
            hjust = -0.15, size = 3) +
  scale_x_log10(expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.15))) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("Larger piece" = "#4C72B0", "Smaller piece" = "#DD8452")) +
  labs(
    title = "First-split piece sizes, round 9062's largest communities",
    subtitle = "Sorted by size of the smaller piece; most balanced at top",
    x = "Nodes in each piece at first split (log scale)",
    y = NULL, fill = NULL
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

Community 56's split (111/47 nodes) is the most balanced of the twelve
by ratio and the strongest remaining candidate for the kind of
title/annotation check performed earlier; community 19's 10/257
anomaly is the strongest candidate for a different kind of check,
since it doesn't fit the balanced-split pattern at all. Neither has
been done yet.

## Cluster labeling

Describing what a community (Girvan-Newman, Louvain, Leiden, or the
k-means centrality clusters) actually contains, in words, independent
of the F1 annotation codebook. Per the "no baseline" stance above, this
is its own independent description of the corpus, standing on its own;
it is not validated against, and does not draw on, the codebook
categories or examples in any form. Comparison against the codebook is
`03_joined_descriptions.qmd`: a separate, later step, so the two stay
apart until then. Not yet run; the method below is settled, the code
is not yet written.

**Independent of any specific GN cut.** The method below takes a
partition as input: any partition, from any community-detection method,
at any cut, with no dependency on which one. It is written to run
against Louvain or Leiden communities as-is, right now, or against
whichever GN cut this document's fragmentation-onset analysis
identifies as usable. Nothing about embedding titles or prompting an
LLM for a description cares which method produced the grouping being
described.

**Why not a direct port of a word-frequency topic model (NMF/LDA).**
These entries' only reliably-available text is `title` (13,760 of
14,328 active entries have a usable title; `abstract` exists on only
232 F1 entries, 1.6% of the corpus, so any method that depends on
abstract text cannot be applied corpus-wide). Titles here average 10.8
words, and the corpus is genuinely multilingual: titles appear in at
least Danish, Norwegian, Swedish, German, English, Russian, Polish,
Icelandic, and Ukrainian across the entries handled during tonight's
correction work alone. Word-frequency methods (NMF, LDA) find structure
by detecting words that co-occur within and across documents; at this
document length, after stopword removal a title typically contributes
5 to 7 content words, which is thin for establishing reliable
co-occurrence statistics, and titles on the same real subject in
different languages share no tokens at all ("gravskik" and "burial
customs" carry the same meaning but no lexical overlap a word-frequency
method can use). This is a structural mismatch between what the method
needs (redundant word co-occurrence across many documents in a shared
vocabulary) and what a corpus of short, cross-linguistic titles can
supply: not a tuning problem correctable by better stopword lists or a
different choice of *k*. Running such a method here risks producing
plausible-looking topics that are actually artifacts of a handful of
shared proper nouns (place names, period terms) rather than genuine
thematic groupings, and no coherence-score threshold distinguishes the
two cases after the fact.

**Method: multilingual sentence embeddings, not word-frequency
factorization.** A multilingual sentence-embedding model encodes each
title as a dense vector positioned by meaning rather than literal word
overlap, which directly addresses both problems above: it needs no
minimum document length to produce a usable vector, and multilingual
models are trained specifically to place semantically equivalent text
from different languages near one another, without a separate
translation step. This trades away the free, interpretable keyword
lists NMF produces as a byproduct of its factorization: an embedding
cluster gives you a group of titles with no automatic explanation of
what unites them. That interpretability work moves entirely onto the
labeling step below, which is a real cost (unlike the CITF email
topic-modeling precedent this method draws loose inspiration from,
where NMF's keyword output already did substantial interpretive work
before any LLM saw the data; see
`zackbatist.info/CITF-emails/topic-modelling`), but is the more honest
match to what title-only, multilingual text can actually support.

**Steps:**

1. **Embed every active entry's title** using a multilingual
   sentence-embedding model (e.g. a `sentence-transformers`
   multilingual model such as `paraphrase-multilingual-mpnet-base-v2`
   or a comparably-scoped alternative; final model choice not yet
   made). Titles only, no abstract text mixed in, so F1 and F2 entries
   are embedded on equal footing rather than giving F1 entries an
   unfair richer signal purely because more of them happen to have an
   abstract.
2. **For each community/cluster under study**, pull the member titles
   and compute each member's cosine distance to the cluster centroid,
   to identify the most centrally-representative titles rather than an
   arbitrary or alphabetical sample.
3. **LLM labeling as a distinct, downstream step**, structurally
   separate from the embedding/clustering step exactly as in the CITF
   precedent (mechanical structure first, interpretive label applied to
   its output after, never the reverse). The prompt supplies only the
   representative titles for one cluster at a time and asks for a short
   thematic description in the model's own words. It does not mention
   the annotation codebook, its categories, or any example labels drawn
   from it, in any form; this is the concrete mechanism by which
   "independent of the codebook" is enforced, not just a stated
   intention.
4. **Stability and model-choice checks before trusting any output**,
   following the CITF precedent: run the labeling prompt across more
   than one model and more than one temperature/seed setting, and treat
   labels that shift substantially across those runs as unstable for
   that cluster rather than averaging or picking one arbitrarily.
5. **Human review of every generated label** against the actual member
   titles before any label is treated as established: the CITF
   precedent's "reviewed and refined by the research team to ensure
   face validity" step, not skipped here.

**Open, not yet decided:**

- Final embedding model choice, and whether to also embed `author`
  affiliation or `booktitle`/`journaltitle` fields alongside `title` as
  weak additional signal, or keep the embedding title-only for the
  cleanest, most consistently-available input across the whole corpus.
- Whether to label every community found at the working GN cut, or only
  the largest N (this document's own GN visualization above already
  makes exactly this call for the *plot*: 12 largest communities
  highlighted, the rest shown as an undifferentiated "other." Labeling
  could follow the same practical threshold, or could aim for full
  coverage; not yet decided).
- Whether the same embedding-and-label pipeline should also run against
  Louvain and Leiden communities as further independent descriptions
  (consistent with treating all three detection methods as separate,
  non-competing readings of the graph throughout this document), or
  whether labeling effort concentrates on the GN partition alone given
  the "camps" question's specific interest in Girvan-Newman's nested,
  nothing-assumed structure.
